sigmoid-curve.context: An S-shaped curve on L-shaped axes that starts flat, climbs through the middle and levels off again. Used for the logistic function, neural network activations and growth that saturates.

exponential-curve.context: A curve on axes that begins nearly flat and then rises sharply toward the upper right. Used for exponential growth, compound interest and viral spread.

logarithmic-curve.context: A curve on axes that shoots up at first and then flattens out toward the right. Used for logarithmic scales, diminishing returns and learning curves.

step-function.context: A staircase of flat steps on axes, each step starting with a solid dot. Used for piecewise constant functions, the floor function and discrete jumps in data.

asymptote.context: A curve bending upward toward a dashed vertical line that it never reaches. Used in calculus and algebra to show a limit or a boundary a graph approaches.

vector-field.context: A ring of small arrows around a central dot, each pointing along the circulation. Used in math and physics for flow, wind, magnetic fields and curl.

complex-plane.context: Crossed horizontal and vertical axes with an arrow from the origin out to a point. Used to plot complex numbers with a real and an imaginary part.

light-cone.context: Two cones meeting tip to tip at a point, the upper cone for the future and the lower for the past. Used in relativity to show which events can affect each other.

feynman-diagram.context: Two lines meeting at a dot, a wavy line running across to a second dot, and two more lines leaving. Used in particle physics to picture how particles exchange a photon.

long-division.context: The long division bracket with a bar across the top, dots for the divisor, dividend digits and a quotient digit. Used for teaching and doing division by hand.

column-addition.context: Two numbers stacked with a plus sign, a line beneath and the total below. Used for teaching written addition and carrying.

factor-tree.context: A ring at the top branching into smaller nodes, ending in solid dots for primes. Used for splitting a number into its prime factors.

ten-frame.context: A two by five frame of cells with counters in the top row. Used in early maths for counting, number bonds to ten and making ten.

number-bond.context: Three linked shapes, one whole at the top joined to two parts below. Used to teach how a number splits into two parts and how parts add to a whole.

pascals-triangle.context: A triangle with rows of dots one, two, three and four wide. Used for binomial coefficients, combinations and number patterns in maths classes.

magic-square.context: A three by three grid with dots on both diagonals and the centre. Used for magic squares, number puzzles and grid games.

truth-table.context: A small grid with a header row and rows of true and false marks under three columns. Used in logic and computing to list every outcome of a Boolean expression.

roman-numerals.context: The Roman numerals I, V and X drawn as plain capitals side by side. Used for numbering on clocks, chapters, dates and outlines.

mayan-numerals.context: A Mayan number shown as two dots above two bars, which reads twelve. Used for the ancient Maya dot and bar counting system.

cuneiform-numerals.context: Five wedge marks in two rows, like the pressed marks of Babylonian numbers. Used for ancient Mesopotamian counting, clay tablets and the history of numbers.

place-value-chart.context: A three column chart with one counter in the first column, two in the second and three in the third. Used to teach hundreds, tens and ones.

decimal-point.context: The number 3.14 with its decimal point drawn as a large dot. Used for decimals, pi, and formatting numbers with fractions.

ordinal-number.context: The number 1 followed by a small raised st. Used for ranking, first place, dates and positions in a list.

odd-and-even.context: Rings of two counters: an even row of two pairs above a row with one left over. Used to teach odd and even numbers and parity.

function-machine.context: A box with an arrow going in on the left, an arrow coming out on the right and a wave inside. Used to explain functions as rules that turn an input into an output.

turing-machine.context: A strip of tape cells with a read and write head pointing down at one cell. Used for the model of computation that reads and writes symbols on a tape.

probability-scale.context: A line scale from 0 to 1 with a down arrow at the halfway point. Used to show how likely an event is, from impossible to certain.

reuleaux-triangle.context: A rounded triangle built from three circular arcs, each centred on the opposite corner. Used as the classic shape of constant width and for guitar picks.

interrobang.context: A question mark whose hook sits over a straight stem with a shared dot, a joined question and exclamation mark. Used for shock mixed with a question.

inverted-question-mark.context: An upside-down question mark with its dot on top. Used at the start of a question in Spanish and Galician.

inverted-exclamation-mark.context: An upside-down exclamation mark with its dot on top and a bar below. Used at the start of an exclamatory sentence in Spanish.

double-exclamation-mark.context: Two exclamation marks side by side, each a bar over a dot. Used for strong emphasis, shouting and excitement.

exclamation-question-mark.context: An exclamation mark followed by a question mark. Used for shocked or confused questions, often written as !?.

semicolon.context: A dot above a comma with a short curved tail. Used to join related clauses and to separate items in complex lists.

colon-punctuation.context: Two dots stacked vertically. Used to introduce lists and explanations, in ratios and times, and as a separator in code.

comma-punctuation.context: A single large comma, a round dot with a curved tail sweeping down and to the left. Used to separate words, list items and clauses.

guillemets.context: A pair of chevrons pointing left beside a pair pointing right. Used as quotation marks in French, Spanish, Russian and many other languages.

lenticular-brackets.context: Two thick crescent-shaped brackets with their straight sides facing each other. Used in Chinese, Japanese and Korean text for titles and emphasis.

dagger.context: A long vertical stroke with one short crossbar near the top. Used as a footnote mark after the asterisk and to mark a death date.

double-dagger.context: A vertical stroke with two short crossbars, one near the top and one near the bottom. Used as the footnote mark that follows the dagger.

asterism-mark.context: Three small asterisks in a triangle, one above and two below. Used to mark a section break or scene break in books.

hedera.context: A heart-shaped ivy leaf with a curling stem. Used as a decorative printer's ornament at the end of a chapter or as a divider.

numero-sign.context: A capital N followed by a small raised o with a bar beneath it. Used as an abbreviation for number in Romance and Slavic languages.

care-of-sign.context: A small c, a slash and a small o written in a row. Used in postal addresses to send mail to someone at another person's address.

sound-recording-copyright.context: A capital P inside a circle. Used on music and audio releases to mark the copyright in a sound recording.

service-mark.context: A raised SM beside two short lines of text. Used to claim a service name as an unregistered mark.

copyleft.context: A reversed C inside a circle, opening to the left. Used as the sign for free licences that require derived works to be shared alike.

ditto-mark.context: A short line of text with two slanted strokes beneath it. Used in lists and ledgers to mean the same as the line above.

tilde.context: A single large smooth wave with one rise and one dip. Used for approximately, the home directory and the swung dash.

backslash.context: A single stroke leaning from the top left to the bottom right. Used in Windows file paths, escape sequences and code.

vertical-bar.context: A vertical bar drawn as two tall strokes with a small gap. Used as the pipe in shells, for logical or and as a divider.

tironian-et.context: A shape like a 7 with a short foot. The old Latin shorthand sign for and, still used in Irish and Scottish Gaelic.

prime-marks.context: A number 1 with a single tick and another 1 with a double tick. Used for feet and inches, minutes and seconds of arc, and derivatives.

estimated-sign.context: A wide lowercase e with a flat crossbar. Used on packaged goods to show that the contents are an average quantity.

acute-accent.context: The letter e with a short slanted stroke rising to the right above it. Used in French, Spanish, Portuguese and many other languages.

circumflex-accent.context: The letter e with a small caret-shaped hat above it. Used in French, Portuguese and Vietnamese to mark vowel quality.

diaeresis.context: The letter e with two dots side by side above it. Used in French and Dutch for a separate vowel sound and as the umlaut in German.

cedilla.context: The letter c with a small hooked tail below it. Used in French, Portuguese and Turkish to soften the c sound.

macron.context: The letter a with a short flat bar above it. Used to mark long vowels in Latin, Maori, Japanese romanisation and dictionaries.

breve.context: The letter a with a small cup-shaped curve above it. Used to mark short vowels in dictionaries and in Romanian and Turkish letters.

ring-above.context: The letter a with a small circle sitting above it. Used in Swedish, Norwegian, Danish and Finnish.

tilde-accent.context: The letter n with a small wavy mark above it. Used in Spanish for the letter enye and in Portuguese for nasal vowels.

ogonek.context: The letter e with a small hook curling to the right at its base. Used in Polish, Lithuanian and Navajo to show a nasal vowel.

double-acute-accent.context: The letter o with two short slanted strokes above it. Used in Hungarian to mark long vowels.

schwa.context: An upside-down lowercase e. Used in phonetics for the neutral, unstressed vowel, as in the a of about.

eszett.context: A tall German letter like a B with an open lower bowl. Used in German for a sharp or double s sound.

thorn-letter.context: A tall vertical stem with a small bowl attached midway on the right. Used in Icelandic and Old English for the th sound.

eth-letter.context: A round bowl with a curved ascender crossed by a short bar. Used in Icelandic, Faroese and Old English for the voiced th sound.

ae-ligature.context: A lowercase a and e joined into one letter with a shared stroke. Used in Danish, Norwegian, Icelandic and Latin words.

oe-ligature.context: A lowercase o and e joined into one letter. Used in French words such as coeur and in Latin-derived spellings.

fi-ligature.context: An f whose hooked top runs into the dot of the i so the two letters form one glyph. Used in typesetting to avoid clashes between letters.

ipa-glottal-stop.context: A question mark shape without its dot, standing on the baseline. Used in phonetics for the catch in the throat, as in uh-oh.

ipa-eng.context: An n whose right leg drops below the line and ends in a hook. Used in phonetics and some African languages for the ng sound, as in sing.

serif-font.context: A capital A with small flat feet at the ends of its strokes. Used to stand for serif typefaces that suit books and long text.

sans-serif-font.context: A capital A with plain strokes and no feet. Used to stand for sans serif typefaces common on screens and in modern design.

monospace-font.context: Three characters with a line under each, all in equal-width cells. Used for fixed-width typefaces in code, terminals and typewriter text.

script-font.context: A flowing handwritten capital letter with a looped tail. Used to stand for script and cursive typefaces in invitations and logos.
